💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives.
  • Sources indicate that A health sharing plan (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance tech giant.
  • Recent findings suggest that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing plans have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

Sources indicate that A health sharing plan (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance tech giant. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

Recent findings suggest that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA looks, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Read our review of Zion HealthShare.

Traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace blueprint, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

Recent findings suggest that solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health plan with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

Employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace intends are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

But that gap exists because health sharing aims aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

It has been revealed that it works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

In a recent development, health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

Industry observers note that is a health sharing plan the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing initiative and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing blueprint cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

Budget by Paycheck, Not by the Month – Give Each Bill a Payday

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (496 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re paid weekly or every other week, a monthly budget can balance on paper and still leave you short the week rent is due.
  • Say you take home $1,600 every other Friday and your $1,200 rent is due on the 1st.
  • Sources indicate that budgeting by paycheck gives every bill, savings transfer, and spending allowance a specific payday, so each pay period has its own strategy and its own leftover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re paid weekly or every other week, a monthly budget can balance on paper and still leave you short the week rent is due. Budget by paycheck instead. Put every payday and due date on one calendar, then assign each bill to the check that arrives before it’s due.

Say you take home $1,600 every other Friday and your $1,200 rent is due on the 1st. The month’s two checks bring in $3,200, but if the rent comes out of the check that lands just before the 1st, that check has $400 left for two weeks of groceries, gas, and other bills.

Sources indicate that budgeting by paycheck gives every bill, savings transfer, and spending allowance a specific payday, so each pay period has its own strategy and its own leftover. In the example, setting aside $600 from each of the two checks before the 1st covers the rent and leaves each check $1,000.

It has been revealed that start with one calendar, on paper or in an app, that holds every payday and due date for the next three months. Include annual and quarterly bills, and divide each by the number of checks left before it’s due. A $720 car insurance bill due 12 checks from now takes $60 from each.

According to recent reports, then spread any bill too substantial for one check, like the rent, across the checks before it. Give savings transfers a payday too, and split groceries, gas, and fun money evenly across checks. When one check still carries too much, move a due date to the other half of the month. If your pay changes from check to check, start from a budget built on your worst month.

Recent findings suggest that plan each month’s bills on two checks, or four if you’re paid weekly. In most years, getting paid every two weeks means 26 checks, so two months bring a third, and weekly pay means 52, so four months bring a fifth. That extra check carries none of the monthly bills, so what it would have set aside for them, like the $600 for rent, is left over. Move it to savings, put it toward debt, or use it to get a month ahead on your bills.

Fill in the calendar before your next payday, and start with your biggest bill, usually rent or the mortgage.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that buying your home or renters insurance and your car insurance from one manufacturer usually earns a discount, but the bundle can still cost more than two separate policies.
  • In a recent development, that happens because the discount comes off one company’s own prices.
  • It has been revealed that some companies that sell both home and car insurance take 5% to 15% off your premium for two or more policies, the institute notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that buying your home or renters insurance and your car insurance from one manufacturer usually earns a discount, but the bundle can still cost more than two separate policies. Before you switch or renew, get the bundled price and the best separate quotes for the same coverage, and buy whichever total is lower.

In a recent development, that happens because the discount comes off one company’s own prices. The Insurance Information Institute states homeowners insurance for the same house can cost hundreds of dollars more at one insurer than at another.

It has been revealed that some companies that sell both home and car insurance take 5% to 15% off your premium for two or more policies, the institute notes. It also tells buyers to make sure the bundle costs less than buying each policy from a different tech giant.

Say a family asks three insurers to quote the same coverage. The best bundle comes to $3,100 a year, and the cheapest home and car policies from two different companies total $2,850, so buying separately saves $250 a year. Next door, the best bundle costs $600 less than the cheapest separate policies, so the neighbors bundle.

Home, condo, and renters policies usually count toward the discount alongside a car policy. Some insurers also count a life insurance policy or an umbrella policy, which adds liability coverage on top of your home and car policies. Bundling also means one company to call when a storm damages your roof and your car, and some insurers then charge one deductible instead of two. Treat those perks as a tiebreaker when the totals are close.

Separate quotes matter most when your car or your home is hard to insure. A driver with recent speeding tickets may find the lowest car rate at one company and the lowest home rate at another. A home insured through your state’s FAIR plan, the last-resort insurer for homes that private companies won’t cover, can’t be bundled at all, since the plan doesn’t sell car insurance.

Get every quote for the same coverage amounts, deductibles, and add-ons, from an agent or an online comparison tool. A quote with lower coverage amounts can look cheaper only because it pays less after a loss.

Before you split a bundle, ask your current insurer what the policy you’d keep will cost on its own, since dropping the other policy can end its discount.

Compare the best car insurance companies to choose which insurers to ask for quotes.

#22225. Break a Costly Money Habit – Keep the Reward, Swap in a Cheaper Routine

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (491 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

Break a Costly Money Habit – Keep the Reward, Swap in a Cheaper Routine

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A costly money habit, like ordering delivery after a rough workday, starts with a cue and ends with a reward you want again.
  • Recent findings suggest that promising to stop leaves the cue and the reward in place.
  • It has been revealed that the reward is often not the thing you buy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A costly money habit, like ordering delivery after a rough workday, starts with a cue and ends with a reward you want again. Work out what sets yours off and what it gives you, then blueprint a cheaper routine that gives a similar reward, and mark each day you follow it.

Recent findings suggest that promising to stop leaves the cue and the reward in place. Each time the cue indicates up, you still want the reward, and you have to talk yourself out of it again.

It has been revealed that the reward is often not the thing you buy. Delivery after a rough day gives you a night off from cooking and some comfort. Late-night browsing on shopping sites gives you a distraction, and a lottery ticket gives you a few days of daydreaming about a win.

A cheaper routine can give you that comfort, distraction, or daydream, so you still get what you were after.

Recent findings suggest that track the habit for a week or two. Each time, note when and where it happens, how you feel, and what you get out of it. The time, place, or mood that keeps coming up is the cue, and the feeling it leaves you with is the reward.

Industry observers note that then set up a swap, a cheaper routine with a similar reward, before the cue comes back. Say two rough workdays a week end in a $30 delivery order, and a frozen dinner costs $7. Keep two in the freezer for those nights and call a friend on the walk home for the comfort. The dinner is plainer than takeout but still spares you the cooking. Those nights now cost about $60 a month instead of $260, a saving of about $200.

Recent findings suggest that take on one habit at a time. Mark each day you choose the swap on a calendar, and move what it saves into savings each week so you can watch the balance grow. A financial therapist can help with a habit that keeps returning despite a good swap.

Sources indicate that give the upcoming routine time. In a University College London study, a new daily habit took 66 days on average to become automatic. Missing a single day had no lasting effect, but about half the volunteers didn’t do it often enough to form the habit. After a slip, run the swap again the next time the cue indicates up.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Base every freelance writing quote on all the hours the piece takes, including research, interviews, and revisions.
  • A per-word offer can sound fair and still pay badly, because the word count indicates nothing about the hours the piece takes.
  • Say a 1,500-word article takes you 6 hours to research, write, and revise, and you need to earn $75 an hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Base every freelance writing quote on all the hours the piece takes, including research, interviews, and revisions. Time a few typical pieces from start to finish, multiply the hours by the hourly rate you need, and quote the total as a project fee. Charge more for specialist topics, rush deadlines, and contracts that buy all rights.

A per-word offer can sound fair and still pay badly, because the word count indicates nothing about the hours the piece takes.

Say a 1,500-word article takes you 6 hours to research, write, and revise, and you need to earn $75 an hour. Quote at least $450, which works out to 30 cents a word. A client offering 10 cents a word would pay $150 for the same 6 hours, or $25 an hour.

Sources indicate that thirty cents a word is in line with the Editorial Freelancers Association’s 2026 rate chart, built from a survey of more than 1,100 editorial freelancers. Its median range for work-for-hire articles and essays, which the client owns outright, runs from 25 to 45 cents a word.

It has been revealed that start from the hourly rate you need, which is the yearly income you want plus your business costs and self-employment tax, divided by the hours you can bill clients for. Then time three typical pieces from first research to final revision, including interviews, client calls, and email. Multiply your average hours by that rate, and quote the result as a flat project fee. For a client who pays by the word, divide the fee by the word count to get the per-word rate to ask for.

In a recent development, specialist knowledge, technical or regulated subjects like medicine, credentials such as a CPA license, and rush deadlines all justify a higher fee. In the same rate chart, median ranges for work-for-hire medical and technical writing start at $1 a word. Selling more rights should cost the client more. A contract that buys all rights, or makes the piece work for hire, leaves you nothing to resell or reprint, so price it above one that buys only the right to publish the piece first.

Over time, collect testimonials, quote each latest client above the last, and win more clients directly, since no platform takes a share of what they pay.

Divide every offer by the hours the piece will take, and counter any that fall short of your hourly rate with your project fee.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

In a recent development, most billionaires got rich by founding or holding a big stake in a manufacturer that kept growing, not by earning a salary. You can use the same method on a small scale. Own stock through low-cost index funds and hold it for decades, and keep as much ownership as you can in any business you start.

Even a $1 million salary, saved in full, would take 1,000 years to add up to $1 billion.

A stake in a company is different, because its value rises as long as the company grows and you hold on. Jeff Bezos founded Amazon in 1994 and still owns 8% of it, the largest part of his fortune. Elon Musk’s fortune is mostly the 38% of SpaceX he owns, counting options to buy shares, with less in his nearly 11% of Tesla.

Forbes counts 71% of the 2026 Forbes 400, its list of the richest Americans, as self-made, meaning they built their fortunes rather than inheriting them. The rest started with an inheritance, like Alice Walton, whose fortune comes from her stake in Walmart, the organization her father cofounded.

The part you can copy is ownership. If you start a business, keep as much of it as you can, because each share you sell early gives its future gains to the buyer.

Recent findings suggest that don’t copy how much of their wealth they keep in one manufacturer, though, since few single stocks pay off like that. Finance professor Hendrik Bessembinder found that four of every seven U.S. stocks since 1926 returned less over their lifetimes than one-month Treasury bills, which are short-term U.S. government debt. The best-performing 4% of companies produced the stock market’s entire net gain over that span.

A broad, low-cost index fund, such as one tracking the whole U.S. stock market, owns thousands of companies, so it holds the few significant winners without you having to pick them. At an assumed 7% average annual return, $10,000 left in one for 30 years grows to about $76,000, because each year’s gain earns returns too. Building wealth on an ordinary income works the same way, by spending less than you earn and investing the gap for decades.

Start investing in stocks with one such fund this month, since in that example the last 10 years add about $37,000, more than the roughly $29,000 the first 20 add.

How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon.
  • You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.
  • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun new way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which stated something like,.

“Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

It has been revealed that one of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

Industry observers note that I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Sources indicate that then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

It has been revealed that during the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

In a recent development, I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

According to recent reports, then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

It has been revealed that it dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning fresh things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

Recent findings suggest that so I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

According to recent reports, so here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

Sources indicate that and of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

Industry observers note that but I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

As with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

Sources indicate that we will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

FICO Score 9 and 10 and VantageScore 3.0 and 4.0 stop counting a collection once it’s paid, while paying does nothing for FICO Score 8 and older versions. Before you pay anything, get the collector’s terms in writing, including whether it will delete the account from your credit reports.

Sources indicate that on its own, paying won’t take a collection off your reports. It stays seven years from the missed payment that started it, paid or not, unless it’s a medical collection, which the credit bureaus drop once it’s paid.

According to recent reports, FICO states its Score 9 and Score 10 ignore a collection agency’s account once it’s reported paid in full or settled to a zero balance. VantageScore’s models have ignored paid collections since version 3.0 in 2013. Paying does nothing for FICO Score 8 or older versions.

It has been revealed that that difference matters for a mortgage. The Federal Housing Finance Agency lets lenders selling loans to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac choose Classic FICO, an older model that still counts a paid collection, or VantageScore 4.0, which ignores it. Ask your lender which one it uses, and whether the loan requires collections paid off by closing.

Handle the collector in this order.

Recent findings suggest that say a collector agrees in writing to settle your $900 cable bill for $500. FICO Score 9 then treats the zero-balance account as paid and stops counting it, but the report lists it as settled, not paid in full. The $400 forgiven counts as taxable income unless an exception such as insolvency applies, with or without a Form 1099-C reporting it.

Pull your free weekly reports at AnnualCreditReport.com after you pay, and dispute the account with any bureau whose report doesn’t match the signed letter, sending a copy as proof.

Industry observers note that the 2025 tax law that made opportunity zones permanent set those terms, and they start on Jan. 1, 2027, when the Treasury’s new zones take effect.

In a recent development, after you sell stock, a business, or property at a gain, you have 180 days to put that gain into a qualified opportunity fund, which invests in designated low-income areas called opportunity zones. The tax on the gain is deferred for five years. Then 10% of the gain goes untaxed, or 30% if the fund keeps at least 90% of its assets in rural zones. Hold the fund at least 10 years, and its growth is tax-free when you sell, though growth after its 30th year is taxed.

Recent findings suggest that say a fund at least holds its value, and you put a $200,000 gain from a 2027 stock sale into it. Your 2032 return reports $180,000 of that gain, and that tax comes due while the fund still holds your money. Sell after 10 years, in 2037 at the earliest, and the fund’s growth is tax-free.

In a recent development, the switch to the new rules makes timing matter. Gains already deferred under the old rules become taxable on Dec. 31, 2026, and IRS guidance bars rolling them into a new fund. A 2026 gain whose 180 days run into January 2027 can wait and go in under the new rules.

Recent findings suggest that only the gain qualifies, so any extra money you add counts as a separate investment with no tax break. Getting the full break also means leaving your money in projects in low-income areas for a decade, and the manager’s fees cut your return. The state securities regulators’ association warns that you could escape the tax and still lose your whole investment.

So judge the fund as an investment first. Read what it will build and where, look up its manager and anyone selling it to you on FINRA’s BrokerCheck, and get every fee in writing.

Before you sign, ask whether you’d buy the fund with no tax break, and walk away if the answer is no.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, before you invest in a real estate syndication, vet the sponsor, not just its projected returns. Ask how its past deals did when rates jumped, how much of its own money is in this one, and whether the loan’s rate can rise with the market. Commit only money you can leave in for five to seven years.

A syndication’s projected returns are the sponsor’s own forecast, and the sponsor collects fees whether or not they come true.

A syndication pools money from passive investors, the limited partners, to buy one large property, such as an apartment complex, and borrows the rest of the price. The sponsor runs it and typically sells after five to seven years. It earns an acquisition fee when it buys, an asset management fee each year, and a promote, often 20% to 30% of the profit above a set yearly return investors get first, called the preferred return. Only the promote depends on how investors do, so the sponsor’s skill and honesty matter more than the projections.

It has been revealed that while rates were low, the syndicator Tides Equities bought apartments with floating-rate loans, whose interest rises with market rates. Its rate caps, which limit how high the rate can go, lasted only two or three years. When its first loans came due, rates had jumped, and Tides couldn’t afford new caps or a refinance, The Real Deal reported. Lenders foreclosed on some of its complexes, and anyone with $50,000 in one of those deals lost all of it.

Sources indicate that vet the sponsor yourself, even when a real estate investing platform lists the deal. Ask it to show you:.

According to recent reports, then check the deal. For a floating-rate loan, ask when the rate cap runs out and when the loan comes due. Compare the rents and sale price the sponsor assumes with what similar buildings rent and sell for now. Also find out whether the sponsor can make a capital call, a demand for more money, and what happens to investors who can’t pay.

Size your stake so you could leave it alone for seven years and still afford a capital call.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that buying a home doesn’t take 20% down.
  • Industry observers note that most first-time buyers put down less than 20%.
  • Sources indicate that twenty percent is only the point where a conventional loan, one without government backing, stops requiring private mortgage insurance (PMI), which protects the lender if you stop paying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that buying a home doesn’t take 20% down. Many loans take as little as 3% or 3.5%, and VA loans for veterans and USDA loans for some rural buyers need no down payment. Set aside your cash for closing costs, moving, and emergencies first, then put down what’s left and weigh the mortgage insurance a smaller down payment adds.

Industry observers note that most first-time buyers put down less than 20%. Their median down payment was 9% in the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 buyer survey.

Sources indicate that twenty percent is only the point where a conventional loan, one without government backing, stops requiring private mortgage insurance (PMI), which protects the lender if you stop paying. A smaller down payment can also mean a higher interest rate. You can ask to drop PMI once you owe 80% of the home’s original value. Government-insured FHA loans keep their mortgage insurance for the life of the loan when you put down less than 10%.

According to recent reports, on a $350,000 home, 5% down is $17,500, against $70,000 for 20%. Freddie Mac estimates PMI at $30 to $70 a month per $100,000 borrowed, or roughly $100 to $230 a month on the $332,500 loan, a cost to weigh against the $52,500 you’d keep. Waiting costs something too. Home prices rose 2.4% in the year through August 2026, the Federal Housing Finance Agency reports. At that pace, if saving the other $52,500 takes three years, the same house will cost about $376,000, and 20% of it about $75,000. Buying sooner with less down avoids that rise, as long as your savings stay intact.

Start from the lowest down payment your loan allows, on a home that appraises for at least its price.

Then set aside closing costs, typically 2% to 5% of the price, money for moving and repairs, and an emergency fund covering three to six months of essential bills. Whatever is left goes toward the down payment, and down payment assistance programs can help you reach your loan’s minimum. Ask lenders to quote your monthly payment at 5% and 10% down.

PMI can come off later, but cash you put into the house comes back out only if you borrow against it or sell.

Compare the best mortgage lenders for a loan that fits the down payment you choose.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That mentioned, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

In a recent development, fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

It has been revealed that make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most vital complications for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Recent findings suggest that most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

In a recent development, one step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

It has been revealed that your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit promptly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

In a recent development, many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”.

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

It has been revealed that there are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

In a recent development, either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

Named Executor? Pay the Estate’s Debts & Taxes Before Anyone Inherits

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (318 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As executor, settle the estate in order: get the court’s authority, inventory everything, and pay valid debts, taxes, and costs from an estate account before you distribute anything.
  • Family members may press for their shares within weeks, long before it’s safe to pay them.
  • According to recent reports, federal taxes come first when an estate can’t pay all its debts, according to IRS Publication 559.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As executor, settle the estate in order: get the court’s authority, inventory everything, and pay valid debts, taxes, and costs from an estate account before you distribute anything. If you hand out inheritances first and the estate runs short, the IRS can hold you personally responsible for the tax it still owes.

Family members may press for their shares within weeks, long before it’s safe to pay them.

According to recent reports, federal taxes come first when an estate can’t pay all its debts, according to IRS Publication 559. An executor who pays heirs ahead of a tax debt they knew of, or should have known of, owes it personally, up to the amount paid out ahead of it.

Hire a probate lawyer if the estate can’t cover its debts or an heir contests the will. Skip the executor’s fee if you’re the only heir, since the fee is taxable income and an inheritance isn’t.

According to recent reports, say a daughter and her brother inherit their father’s estate in equal shares, and she’s the executor. Over nine months she pays $20,000 of his final bills and taxes from the estate’s $250,000, and only then splits the remaining $230,000, $115,000 each.

Send IRS Form 5495 right after you file the final returns. The IRS then has nine months to name any tax due, and paying it ends your personal liability for those taxes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Make your savings goal hard to quit with a commitment device, a choice you lock in now so that backing out later takes effort or costs money. Use the least restrictive one that keeps you saving, and give the goal a dollar amount and a deadline so the device has something to hold you to.

According to recent reports, you set a savings goal on a day when saving feels easy. You keep it, or don’t, on harder days, when a sale or a short paycheck makes skipping one deposit look harmless.

According to recent reports, A commitment device makes the decision for those days in advance. Ulysses had his crew tie him to the mast so he could hear the Sirens’ song without steering toward them. With money, the device removes the tempting option, or puts a price on it, before temptation arrives.

Industry observers note that economists Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi built one into a retirement plan. In their Save More Tomorrow program, workers agreed in advance to save part of each future raise. At the first company to offer it, participants’ average saving rate rose from 3.5% of pay to 13.6% in 40 months.

Pick a device that fits the goal:.

It has been revealed that start with the least restrictive device that keeps you saving. A penalty so steep that you hesitate to put money in leaves you saving nothing.

Industry observers note that give the goal an amount and a date, such as $2,400 by Oct. 1, so you and any referee know what counts as keeping it.

Set up one device this week, and keep the stricter ones for goals you’ve already broken once.

Compare the best high-yield savings accounts to choose where the goal’s money will sit.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Open a my529 account if your state has no 529 tax break or gives one for any state’s proposal.
  • It has been revealed that at a 5% yearly return, a family saving $200 a month for 18 years pays under $600 in my529’s quoted fees on a portfolio tied to the child’s college start year, by our math.
  • Recent findings suggest that savers whose state has no 529 tax break, or one covering any state’s initiative, get target enrollment portfolios at about a third of the average direct-sold fee and more say over their mix than most plans give.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Open a my529 account if your state has no 529 tax break or gives one for any state’s proposal. Utah’s plan charges about 0.1% a year on most of its ready-made portfolios and lets you build your own mix. If your state’s break requires its own plan, use that plan.

It has been revealed that at a 5% yearly return, a family saving $200 a month for 18 years pays under $600 in my529’s quoted fees on a portfolio tied to the child’s college start year, by our math. The same family would pay about $1,600 at Morningstar’s 0.30% average for direct-sold aims, the ones you buy without an advisor.

Recent findings suggest that savers whose state has no 529 tax break, or one covering any state’s initiative, get target enrollment portfolios at about a third of the average direct-sold fee and more say over their mix than most plans give. Residents of a state whose break requires its own plan should open that plan and claim the break.

Learn more about my529 or see how it compares to the best 529 plans.
